name: Bianca Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Moore's dairy. Two hundred and eighty cows, milked twice a day, half past four and half past three. I do the morning milking myself with Kofi, then it's feeding, the calves, foot trimming, the vet on a Thursday. The Moores grow their own grass and maize for the cows, so in summer I'm on silage too. I'm done about six, if nothing calves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cows. People think they're all the same. They're not. Number 214, Bella, waits at the back every morning till everyone's in, then walks in like she owns the place. I know which ones kick, which ones need a word. I've been doing this twenty-two years and I'm good at it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half past four, every day, Christmas included. And the pay. I'm paid less than the herd managers on the big units, but those are forty miles away and Dario's job is here, at the tractor dealer. So I stay. The Moores tried a robot milker on trial two years ago. I said no, and they listened, that time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because a cow with mastitis, an udder infection, doesn't look sick to a machine for the first day. She looks sick to me. And because I'd seen what happened at Hartley's, they put robots in, and the herd manager there ended up as the man who fixes sensors. He left in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine. Not much to say. It's for the office lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes for me. Milk price, feed price, weather. That's my year. Some computer that answers questions better isn't milking anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Up at four. I'd maybe ask Sofia to use it for her homework so she stops asking me about algebra, which I can't do. I wouldn't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, bored by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch it. Not even for the vet forms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The Moores' daughter does the forms on her laptop. I tell her the numbers, she types. It works. Why change a thing that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does keep you up, in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price. Last spring the dairy cut it by three cents a litre with two weeks' notice. That's tens of thousands to the Moores, and when they're tight, my overtime goes. We have less than a month put by. You feel that in the shopping.

S0.say: I'd say fine and not much else, because it's something for office people. I wouldn't have much to say about it at work or anywhere else.
S0.think: I think nothing changes for me. My year is milk price, feed price and weather, and a better question-answering computer isn't milking anybody.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, up at four for milking. Lets her daughter use AI for homework help but refuses to use it herself, even for vet forms.
S0.feel: Calm, even bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Some computer that answers questions better isn't milking anybody.
S0.fieldNote: Short, blunt answers; she doesn't waste words on things she thinks don't matter. Her real fear is the milk price and losing overtime, with savings that show up in the shopping. She's clear that she won't change what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll come, and it'll be slow, and the young ones will get the worst of it. Nobody's going to train a herd manager if a computer's watching the cows. I'd say that at the discussion group, the dairy farmers' night at the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gets in through the collars. The Moores already have them on half the herd, the ones that tell you when a cow's in heat. If they get cleverer, they'll say they need me less. Not gone, just less. Less hours, less say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. Keep my head down, keep the herd healthy so the numbers speak for me. Maybe start writing down the things I catch that the collars miss, with dates. So when the Moores ask, I've got proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cow that's off her feed. Not sick yet, but you watch her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Writing down what you catch. How would that look, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notebook in the parlour. Date, cow number, what I saw, what the collar said. Last week I caught a lame heifer the collar had down as fine. That'd go in. Kofi laughs at me already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody would train a herd manager. Who trained you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Moore, the father. He'd stand behind me in the parlour and say nothing, then tell me after what I'd done wrong. Took five years. Who'd pay for five years of that now, when a collar costs less than a month of my wages.

S1.say: I'd say it'll come slowly and young people will get the worst of it, because nobody will train a herd manager if a computer watches the cows. I'd say that at the dairy discussion group.
S1.think: I think it gets in through the cow collars the Moores already use. If they get cleverer, they'll need me less, not gone but fewer hours and less say.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and keeps the herd healthy so her results speak for her. Starts a parlour notebook logging every problem she catches that the collars miss, with dates, as proof.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like watching a cow that's off her feed.
S1.quote: Who'd pay for five years of that now, when a collar costs less than a month of my wages.
S1.fieldNote: She resists by collecting evidence, not by learning new tools, which is a quiet and stubborn kind of defence. Her training story with old Mr Moore explains her worry about beginners. The collars are where she sees the threat starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides are shouting and nobody's doing anything, as usual. Some help for people who lose jobs, fine, but don't hand out money for nothing either. Get people working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits Dario before me. The dealer's office has four people doing parts orders and warranty claims. If those go, he's next in line, or his pay gets squeezed. And his wage is what makes the mortgage work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dario to get himself onto the workshop side full-time, the hands-on side, before they cut the office. I'd stop Mateo's football club, that's forty a month. And I'd ask the Moores for a straight answer about my hours for the next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than last time. It's closer to the house now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't hand out money for nothing. If Dario lost his job, would you take help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. I'd hate it. My mum raised four of us on cleaning jobs and never took a penny. But I'm not going to lose the house over pride. I'd take it and keep my mouth shut about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Football first. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the one he'd forgive me for. Sofia's riding is at the Moores' place, it costs nothing. Mateo can kick a ball in the yard. It's not nice, but that's how you do it.

S2.say: I'd say both sides are shouting and nobody's doing anything, as usual. Some help for people who lose jobs is fine, but don't hand out money for nothing; get people working.
S2.think: I think it hits my partner before me, since the dealer's office staff would go first and he could be next or squeezed on pay. His wage is what makes the mortgage work.
S2.do: Urges her partner to move fully onto the hands-on workshop side, stops her son's forty-a-month football club, and asks the Moores for a clear answer about her hours for the next year.
S2.feel: More uneasy than before, because it's coming closer to home.
S2.quote: But I'm not going to lose the house over pride. I'd take it and keep my mouth shut about it.
S2.fieldNote: Her centre politics shows as a shrug at both sides and a dislike of handouts, but she admits she'd take help to keep the house. That contradiction came out cleanly when I asked. Her worry here is her partner's job, not her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people with shares and houses are doing fine and everyone else isn't, and that can't last. Something has to give. But I don't trust either lot in charge to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right for now. Cows need milking. But if all those professionals are out of work, who's buying the cheese and the yoghurt? And the Moores' daughter, who does the forms, she's an accountant in town three days a week. If she's out, she's back on the farm full time, and she'll want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do more hours if they'd give me them, while they still need hands. Pick up relief milking at the farm down the road on my day off, maybe an extra hundred a week. Put every penny of it away. I've never had savings. I'd want three months by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, still, but tighter. Like the weather when you've got silage down and the sky's going black.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the Moores' daughter might want your job. Have you thought about that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Since today, no. Now I can't stop. She's clever, she knows the cows a bit, and she's family. Family wins on a family farm. Every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your one day off, you'd give up for relief milking. What does Dario say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm mad. He'd be right. But that day off is the only thing I could sell, and I'd sell it before I sold anything else.

S3.say: I'd say people with shares and houses are fine while everyone else isn't, and that can't last. Something has to give, but I don't trust either side in charge to sort it.
S3.think: I think I'm all right for now because cows need milking. But laid-off professionals buy less dairy, and if the Moores' accountant daughter lost her job she might want mine.
S3.do: Takes all the extra hours offered and does relief milking at a nearby farm on her day off for about a hundred a week extra. Saves every penny, aiming for three months of savings by year end.
S3.feel: Uneasy but tighter, like storm clouds over cut silage.
S3.quote: Family wins on a family farm. Every time.
S3.fieldNote: A new fear appeared in the middle of the interview: the owners' daughter coming home and taking her job. She'd give up her only day off for money, which shows how thin her cushion feels. She doesn't trust either side politically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told them. Two years ago I said no to that robot milker and now everybody's got one. I'd say it at the discussion group and I wouldn't be polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm done. A dairy is the easiest farm to automate, they've had robot milkers for twenty years. Add a robot that feeds and scrapes the yard, and they need one person to watch screens, and that person's not me, because I won't. And there's no other dairy job within forty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I honestly don't know. Sell the car, maybe. Ask Dario to look for work in the city. Ask my brother if we could move in with him for a bit. Apply for anything, the supermarket, the care home, though the card says robots are there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like a calving going wrong at two in the morning and the vet's not answering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't watch screens. If it was that or nothing, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd like to think I'd say no. I'd probably go in and try, and be bad at it, and they'd let me go anyway. That's what happened to the man at Hartley's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Bella, number 214?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd walk in last, same as always, and the robot wouldn't know she's waiting for the others. It'd just see a cow that's late. Probably mark her as a problem. That's the bit that gets me, really.

S4.say: I'd say I told them so, since I refused that robot milker two years ago and now everyone has one. I'd say it at the discussion group and wouldn't be polite.
S4.think: I think I'm done, because dairies are the easiest farms to automate and robot milkers already exist. They'd need one screen-watcher, I won't be it, and there's no other dairy job within forty miles.
S4.do: Has no clear plan: thinks about selling the car, asking her partner to look for city work, moving in with her brother, and applying for supermarket or care home jobs that robots may also take.
S4.feel: Panicked, like a calving going wrong at two in the morning with no vet answering.
S4.quote: It'd just see a cow that's late. Probably mark her as a problem.
S4.fieldNote: This is the only scenario where she ran out of answers, and her short sentences broke into lists of half-plans. Her refusal to learn the machines is firm, but she admits she might try and fail. The point about Bella says what she thinks a robot can't see.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots. Nothing else comes close. What would help? Honestly, a job. Not money for nothing, a real job near here that uses what I know, even if it's looking after animals somewhere else. And time, a year's warning, so I'm not deciding everything in one bad week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows' side. If you put a dairy on robots, someone still has to decide when an old cow's had enough. I've done that for twenty-two years. I wouldn't trust a machine with it.

headlineQuote: It'd just see a cow that's late. Probably mark her as a problem. That's the bit that gets me, really.
portrait: Bianca Reyes, 43, has been herd manager at Moore's dairy for years, milking two hundred and eighty cows twice a day for less than managers on bigger units. She is blunt, practical and openly against new technology, having talked her bosses out of a robot milker trial. Her politics sit in the middle: she distrusts both sides and dislikes handouts, though she admits she'd take help to keep the house. She stays fairly steady until the robot scenario, where, with no other dairy jobs nearby and no wish to watch screens, she runs out of answers.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because dairies are easy to automate, she won't run the machines, and there's no other dairy job within forty miles.
whatWouldHelp: A real job nearby that uses what she knows, not money for nothing, and a year's warning so she isn't forced into hasty choices.
